name: Hassan Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is a bit of everything. I'm training to be a secondary school PE teacher, so I'm in lectures on how the body works and how kids learn, and twice a week we're on the pitch coaching each other. I lifeguard at the leisure centre on Wednesday evenings and Sunday mornings. Saturdays I coach an under-tens football team, unpaid, which is the best part of my week. I live with my dad, who's a car mechanic, and my younger sister.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What kind of teacher do you want to be?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're not struggling, but we're careful. Dad's garage is quiet in winter, and my mum passed away a few years ago, so it's the three of us. The loan pays my fees. The lifeguarding covers my bus and lunches, and I've got about two weeks of spending saved. I got in with average grades, no scholarship. I'm not the cleverest, but I'm reliable, and teachers say that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. I've never thought it was going to change everything overnight. I'd tell the lads at the leisure centre it's overhyped, and that people have always worried about new machines. I'd probably say that if my work's honest, I'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit relieved. Teaching is about turning up and caring about kids, and that stays the same. But I still worry about money and about getting a permanent job, because PE posts are few. It's the same worry I've got today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Lectures, lifeguarding, football on Saturdays. I'd use the AI tool the way I do now, now and then, to plan a lesson and then rewrite it so it sounds like me. I'd ask the leisure centre for more shifts, and I'd start looking at which schools near us have PE vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not dramatic. A bit like being on a steady jog, you know it's going to be long but you're settled into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now, if at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, mostly for lesson plans. I ask it for a warm-up that suits twelve-year-olds in a small hall, and it gives me a start. I change it. It once told me to run a drill that would've gotten kids hurt, so I'm careful. I don't trust it with anything where a child's safety is involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worry you carry that AI doesn't touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad is fifty-six, and his back is going. If he can't work, we lose half our income. He doesn't talk about it, but I see him wince under a car. That's the one that keeps me awake, and nothing about AI changes it.

say: I'd tell the lads at the leisure centre it's **overhyped**, and people have always worried about new machines.
I'd say honest work will see me through.
think: Teaching is about **turning up** and caring about kids, and that stays the same.
I still worry about **money** and getting a permanent PE post, which are few.
do: Carry on with lectures, **lifeguarding** and Saturday football coaching.
Use AI for **lesson plans** and rewrite them in my own voice.
Check which local schools have **PE vacancies**.
feel: **Okay** and not dramatic, like settling into a long steady jog.
S0.quote: Dad is fifty-six, and his back is going. If he can't work, we lose half our income.
fieldNote: Hassan's biggest pressure is his **dad's health** and the household income.
He uses AI **now and then**, and has a story about it suggesting an unsafe drill.
His anxiety is **personal and practical**, not about technology.

steps.text: Keep lifeguarding and coaching the under-tens on Saturdays
Use AI for lesson plans and rewrite them in my voice
Check which local schools have PE vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change things, but you can't learn to swim from a screen. I'd tell my friends to stick with jobs that need hands and presence. And I'd say people should be allowed to work and earn, not just be told what to do or given handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit uneasy. Lifeguarding is already moving towards cameras that spot swimmers in trouble, and the leisure centre manager talks about it. A school might also use software to plan lessons and track fitness. So the sorts of jobs I do on the side might shrink, but the teaching itself seems safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the planning tools properly now, so I'm the trainee who uses them well. I'd sign up for extra coaching qualifications, like a swimming teacher award, because that's useful and hands-on. I'd keep lifeguarding as long as they need me. And I'd save a bit from every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I can see good bits and bad bits. I feel I can cope if I do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of a PE teacher's job could AI take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lesson plans, fitness tracking, report comments. A good tool would do those in minutes. That would leave me more time on the pitch with kids, which is the part I love. The danger is schools deciding a teacher doesn't need an assistant or a technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the leisure centre cut staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the manager and ask about moving into swim teaching. It needs a person in the water, and parents like that. I'd say it's an honest job, and I'd rather do that than sit around.

say: I'd tell friends to stick with jobs that need **hands and presence**, since nobody learns to swim from a screen.
I'd say people should be allowed to **work and earn**, not just get handouts.
think: Cameras that spot swimmers could shrink **lifeguarding**, but teaching itself seems safe.
I'm a bit **uneasy** about schools cutting assistants and technicians.
do: Sign up for a **swimming teacher** award.
feel: **Fine** and a bit restless, able to cope if I do the work.
S1.quote: Lesson plans, fitness tracking, report comments. A good tool would do those in minutes.
fieldNote: Hassan sees AI as **useful help** that frees time for the part of teaching he loves.
His **free-market** instinct: people should work and earn, not be handed things.
He moves towards a hands-on qualification, swim teaching, rather than a new field.

steps.text: Learn the lesson-planning tools properly this term
Sign up for a swimming teacher award
Save ten pounds from every lifeguard shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot to take in and nobody's ready. I'd say people have to be allowed to earn their way through it, not wait for someone to hand it to them, but that employers and governments need to give people time. Two years is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. The leisure centre job would be gone quickly, and the school might cut posts when AI plans lessons. And Dad's garage might lose customers when cars drive themselves. We'd lose income from all directions. I'd have no savings and just over two years of degree left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dad and my sister the same night. Then I'd work every shift going and save everything. I'd ask the university whether students on placements are paid. I'd look for hands-on work that still needs people, like coaching or swimming lessons. And I'd keep studying, because standing still is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted and a bit stunned. Like when you're one-nil up and the other side scores twice in a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight: Dad, it's going to be tight, but I'm not quitting. I'd say we need to look at what we could cut together. He'd say don't worry about me, finish your studies. But he'd be worried too, and we'd both know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap matter for PE teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. Schools need people in the gym to keep kids safe, and robots that can do that are years away. So the teaching job might last longer than most. But I'd need to reach the end of the degree first, and that's the problem.

say: I'd say **two years** is not enough, and governments and employers must give people time.
I'd say people should earn their way through it, **not wait for handouts**.
think: It scares me: the leisure centre job goes, schools may cut posts and **Dad's garage** may lose customers.
I'd have **no savings** and over two years of degree left.
do: Talk to **Dad and my sister** the same night.
Work every **shift** going and save everything.
Ask whether students on **placements** are paid.
feel: **Gutted** and stunned, like the other side scored twice in a minute.
S2.quote: Schools need people in the gym to keep kids safe, and robots that can do that are years away.
fieldNote: Hassan is **alarmed** because income could fall in three places: his job, a school post and his dad's garage.
He keeps his **work-ethic framing** but accepts governments must give time.
He stays practical: shifts, savings, family talk.

steps.text: Work every lifeguard shift going and save the pay
Talk with Dad and my sister about bills that night
Ask the university whether placement students are paid
Keep studying and coaching the under-tens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people a fair shot if they get on with it. I'd say governments should help people who retrain, but also leave room for those who want to start their own thing. I'd tell my mates to pick a trade or a skill and get good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel decent. I'd finish my degree in three years, then get two years of teaching, and PE is a hands-on job. If I get a permanent post, that's the real safety. I'd still worry about Dad, because the garage might feel it before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, pass the teaching induction, and take any PE job going, even in a different town. I'd pick up swimming teacher and first aid awards, because every school wants them. I'd save for a car. And I'd help Dad think about taking on an apprentice or an electric car certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious. Like waiting for the second half to start, you know there's a game still to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra three years let me qualify and get a salary. Two years, I'd still be a student chasing shifts. With five years, I'd be a teacher with a pay slip and a pension. That's the thing that matters to someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your plan for the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply early to schools and be willing to move. I'd get references from the football club and the leisure centre. It's a long shot to get a post in my home town, so I'd think about going to wherever there's a vacancy, even if it means leaving Dad for a bit.

say: I'd say five years gives people a **fair shot** if they get on with it.
I'd tell mates to pick a **trade or skill** and get good at it.
think: I'd feel decent: I'd qualify and teach a hands-on subject, with a **permanent post** as the real safety.
I'd worry about **Dad's garage** feeling it before 2034.
do: Finish the degree, pass induction and take any **PE job** going.
Pick up **swimming teacher** and first aid awards.
Help Dad look at an **electric car** certificate.
feel: **Cautious**, like waiting for the second half to start.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd be a teacher with a pay slip and a pension. That's the thing that matters to someone like me.
fieldNote: Hassan measures security in a **pay slip**, a pension, a traditional yardstick.
He is willing to **move** for a post, even if it means leaving his dad for a while.
Uneasy because the family garage is exposed and he has no cushion yet.

steps.text: Apply early to schools and take any PE job going
Pick up swimming teacher and first aid awards
Move to wherever a PE vacancy exists
Help Dad look at an electric car certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good run. I'd tell people it's time to get skilled, save and look after your family, and not leave it to the state. I'd say we've had big changes before and honest workers got through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fine. I'd qualify, teach for a few years, maybe become head of PE by thirty. By 2036 I'd be settled, and hands-on work lasts a few years longer. I'd worry about Dad retiring before then, but with ten years I could help look after him properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a teaching job, and save. I'd keep coaching football, because it's the heart of why I'm doing this. I'd learn new tools as they prove themselves. I'd put a deposit down on a small house. And I'd help my sister through school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Right now I don't feel calm about much, but this one feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the teacher kids remember. I'd get a coaching badge for older kids, and maybe run a youth team. If the world gets wobbly, kids will need someone steady in the gym who says, you can do this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister not to follow what's fashionable. Learn something real, work hard, be kind. I'd say Dad and I will be there. And I'd say don't be afraid of new things, just wait until they're proven.

say: I'd say ten years is a **good run**, so get skilled, save and look after family.
I'd say honest workers got through **big changes** before.
think: I'd feel fine: **qualify**, teach for years and maybe lead PE by thirty.
With ten years I could help look after **Dad** properly.
do: Finish the degree, get a **teaching job** and save.
Keep **coaching football**, because it's the heart of why I'm doing this.
Put a **deposit** on a small house.
S4.quote: If the world gets wobbly, kids will need someone steady in the gym who says, you can do this.
fieldNote: Hassan feels **calm** because the picture offers a teaching salary and time to help his dad.
His identity is the **steady coach**, which anchors him in every scenario.
He wants to wait until tools are **proven** before adopting them, true to his steady style.

steps.text: Get a teaching job and keep coaching football
Save for a deposit on a small house
Help my sister through school and look after Dad

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole family's income would wobble at once, and I'd be mid-degree. What would help is a decent bursary for teacher trainees, paid placements, and clear word from schools about whether PE posts will exist. I'd also want help for small garages like Dad's, so they can change at their own speed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that people like me aren't asking for handouts. Give us a fair chance to work, and some time. That's all.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't asking for handouts. Give us a fair chance to work, and some time.
portrait: Hassan is **19**, a first-year PE teacher trainee who lifeguards and coaches an under-tens football team, living with his dad and sister.
He is a traditional, work-minded voice who favours **earning over handouts** but accepts governments should give time.
He uses AI **now and then** for lesson plans and distrusts it where children's safety is involved.
His mood runs from anxious to **alarmed** when family income is at risk, and **calm** with ten years.
His anchor is the **steady coach** he wants to be, and a teaching salary.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because the whole family's income would wobble at once.
whatWouldHelp: A bursary for **teacher trainees**, paid placements and support for small garages like his dad's.
